items.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023
items.q: And then David Taylor, the bass trombone player in the band, who is a virtuoso player, he does a lot of avant garde classical stuff.

ctx.x: Those — I think you said 13 new charts you wrote, can you describe where the initial idea, how it arrives in your head? Is there a — do you say it’s time to write a funk chart, or gee I haven’t written a jazz waltz in a while? How does it percolate?

Well those things happen but you know like for instance one of the tunes on the album is called “Fat Man.” And it was written probably in the mid-70s. And my friend, Joe Randazzo, who was my best friend, a great bass trombone player in New York, that was a heavy cat for the first half of his life. And then he went into like Weight Watchers — or got into a program and he was slim for the rest of his life. But that tune, “Fat Man” is a slow, sort of a bluesy kind of tune. And it’s been sitting around. And then he…

“Amigion.” So I used that as a canon. And it’s fast you know. And after a shout chorus it goes into this canon where different sections of the band — and it works out great you know. So every song for me has its own harmonic ambiance that I don’t want to go outside of, and it has themes in it that I can use as harmony parts, take segments of the melody and use those segments as back-up harmony so that instead of having a stock voicing the voicing is derived from the melody itself. And so it’s a combination of…
